quick.summary: How to handle aggressive pushback on your project without getting defensive.
quick.takeaway: Validate a piece of their concern first, then add your own evidence.

parts.title: Find common ground

beats.line: They said my cloud plan costs too much. Why did I completely freeze?
Imagine driving a car. Suddenly your passenger yanks the steering wheel.
I would grab it right back so we do not crash.
And fighting over the wheel is exactly what causes the crash.
When they push back, your brain treats it like a physical attack.
Can I just say find common ground?
Spot on. You have to agree with a piece of their worry.
But how do I agree without saying my whole plan is garbage?

parts.cliff: How to agree without throwing your whole plan away.

beats.line: You validate the feeling, not the conclusion.
Like saying that cost is a totally fair thing to watch.
Exactly. It lowers their guard and puts you back on the same team.
Then you add your evidence instead of just fighting theirs.
Say yes, and here is how it pays off over time.
So I say they are right about short term costs.
You are adding a new fact to the map they already drew.
Then I show the long term savings we gain later.
You steer the car together instead of fighting for the wheel.

quiz.question: Someone says your migration timeline is completely unrealistic. How do you respond?
options: Tell them they do not understand the details.
Agree that speed introduces a lot of risk.
Immediately offer to add three more weeks.
Walk away to avoid a pointless argument.
quiz.explanation: Agreeing with the feeling lowers their guard. Then you can add your evidence about how you will mitigate the risk.

quiz.question: When you validate a stakeholder's feeling, you are agreeing that their conclusion is correct.
quiz.explanation: You can validate that cost is important without agreeing that your plan is too expensive.
